title: How far can you jump?
hook: a hundred yojanas of water, and a circle of monkeys saying out loud how far each of them can jump
carry: satya: say what you can really do

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati's wings grew back as he told the monkeys where Sita was. Seva heals the one who serves.

The job is finally clear, and it's impossible. Sita is in Lanka, an island a hundred yojanas across the ocean. A yojana is an old measure of distance, many miles long. The monkeys walk down to the shore and look at the water. Valmiki describes it like something alive: huge waves, sea creatures, a roar that never stops. The whole army sits down on the sand, quiet. Nobody wants to say the obvious thing first.
screen: `THE JOB IS CLEAR.` → `A HUNDRED YOJANAS OF SEA.` → `THE ARMY SITS DOWN, QUIET.`

segments.voice: Angada, the young prince who leads them, breaks the silence: who here can cross this? One by one, the monkeys answer honestly. One says he can leap ten yojanas. Another, twenty. Another, thirty. On it goes, each a little further, up to the old bear Jambavan, who says ninety. When he was young, he adds, he could have done it easily. He once circled the great god Vishnu when Vishnu strode across the worlds in three steps. But age has taken that. Then Angada speaks. He thinks he can jump the full hundred. What he isn't sure of is the jump back. Jambavan answers kindly but firmly. You're the leader, the root of the whole expedition. You don't send the root. Nobody brags here, and nobody pretends. That's a Hindu virtue with a name: satya, truthfulness. In yoga it's one of the yamas, the first restraints a student is asked to keep. And satya isn't only about not lying to others. It's not lying about yourself: not puffing up your number, and not shrinking it either. Every monkey on that beach tells the truth, the numbers fall short, and that's allowed. Honest limits are how the right one gets found. This week: a guest fed like a god, a gift that asked nothing, despair on the shore, water for a brother, ego and love, seva, and now satya. One monkey hasn't spoken. He's sitting apart, saying nothing at all.
screen: `WHO CAN CROSS THIS?` · `TEN, TWENTY, THIRTY... NINETY.` · `ANGADA: I'M NOT SURE OF THE WAY BACK.` · then, large: `SATYA: THE HONEST NUMBER.` · then: `ONE MONKEY HASN'T SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that feels too far to cross: a task, a conversation, a long recovery. Instead of measuring the whole distance, ask honestly how far you can go today, ten yojanas or twenty, and hold that number without shame and without puffing it up. That's satya, turned toward yourself. With each breath out, let the gap between what you can do and what is needed simply be true, for now.
Yojana, an old measure of distance many miles long: what the monkeys count in as each says how far he can jump, and the numbers fall short of a hundred.
Your line: satya, say what you can really do. Not a hundred yet, anyway. Day six hundred two, done.

screen: `DAY 602 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LEAP DECIDED, PART TWO.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Kishkindha Kanda often linger on this scene of the monkeys stating their limits on the shore, because it sets up the moment when Jambavan turns to Hanuman.

fork.reveal: each monkey gives his true number: satya, honest about himself, neither puffed up nor hidden.

original.note: Sanskrit yojana, an old unit of distance; its exact length varies by source.

trapdoor: what you thought: the monkeys were all heroes who could do anything.
what it means: each one names an honest limit, satya about himself, and none of the numbers reaches a hundred.
what a scholar hears: Jambavan's memory of circling Vishnu's three strides points to the Vamana story of Vishnu's three strides across the worlds, a story told in other Hindu texts as well.
recall: a finger-ring with Rama's name on it
